Entropic Regularization: Convergence

This chapter focuses on algorithmic convergence for entropic optimal transport: the marginals and the temperature are fixed, and one asks how Sinkhorn iterates, soft transforms and related monotone scaling procedures approach their regularized fixed point. Statistical convergence is a separate question, because the empirical marginals then change with the sample size; this is the topic of Paragraph.

The chapter revisits Sinkhorn convergence through several complementary lenses. Bregman projections explain the alternating-projection geometry, Fortet’s order argument gives qualitative fixed-point convergence, and an order-theoretic M-function viewpoint explains why Sinkhorn-like scaling can still converge even when the equations are no longer the gradient of a convex potential. Robust Bregman estimates then give a non-asymptotic dual-gap bound, while Hilbert’s metric gives a clean linear contraction when the kernel is uniformly positive. The last sections discuss Gaussian closed forms and continuous ε\varepsilonε-Sinkhorn flows as model cases where the fixed-point structure becomes explicit.

Guiding Comparison

There are three useful convergence stories for Sinkhorn. Bregman projections explain the geometry of alternating row and column corrections; Fortet’s monotone argument explains qualitative fixed-point convergence of soft transforms; Hilbert’s projective metric gives a linear contraction when the kernel is uniformly positive. A fourth, more algebraic story views Sinkhorn as a monotone coordinate-clearing system, which survives beyond variational OT. The statistical behavior of empirical OT and empirical Sinkhorn losses is treated separately in the next chapter.

Sinkhorn Convergence: Bregman Point of View¶

Sinkhorn can be read as alternating Bregman projections. The main geometric message is simple: each row or column rescaling is the KL projection onto one affine marginal constraint. The convergence mechanism then follows from the Pythagorean identity for Bregman divergences.

For simplicity, this section is written for discrete measures. The same ideas carry over to general measures, and the robust-rate section below expresses the constants through cost and potential oscillations rather than through the number of grid points.

Alternating KL Projections¶

The projection viewpoint explains Sinkhorn as repeated enforcement of one marginal constraint at a time. It is not specific to entropy, although KL is the case where the projections reduce to elementary row and column scalings.

The following matrix construction is the finite-dimensional counterpart of the measure-valued Definition: Measure Bregman Divergence.

Definition: Bregman Divergence

Let Ω⊂Rn×m\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n\times m}Ω⊂Rn×m be convex with nonempty interior, and let Φ:Rn×m→R∪{+∞}\Phi:\mathbb R^{n\times m}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}Φ:Rn×m→R∪{+∞} be a proper lower-semicontinuous Legendre function with dom⁡(Φ)=Ω\operatorname{dom}(\Phi)=\Omegadom(Φ)=Ω. Thus Φ=+∞\Phi=+\inftyΦ=+∞ outside Ω\OmegaΩ, while Φ\PhiΦ is differentiable and strictly convex on int⁡(Ω)\operatorname{int}(\Omega)int(Ω). For P,Q∈int⁡(Ω)\P,Q\in\operatorname{int}(\Omega)P,Q∈int(Ω), the Bregman divergence generated by Φ\PhiΦ is

BΦ(P∣Q):=Φ(P)−Φ(Q)−⟨∇Φ(Q),P−Q⟩.B_\Phi(\P\mid Q) \eqdef \Phi(\P)-\Phi(Q)-\langle \nabla\Phi(Q),\P-Q\rangle .BΦ​(P∣Q):=Φ(P)−Φ(Q)−⟨∇Φ(Q),P−Q⟩.
(1)

For the quadratic generator Φ(P)=12∥P∥F2\Phi(\P)=\frac12\|\P\|_{\mathrm F}^2Φ(P)=21​∥P∥F2​ on Rn×m\mathbb R^{n\times m}Rn×m, one recovers half the squared Euclidean distance, BΦ(P∣Q)=12∥P−Q∥F2B_\Phi(\P\mid Q)=\frac12\|\P-Q\|_{\mathrm F}^2BΦ​(P∣Q)=21​∥P−Q∥F2​. For the negative entropy Φ(P)=∑i,jPi,jlog⁡Pi,j\Phi(\P)=\sum_{i,j}\P_{i,j}\log \P_{i,j}Φ(P)=∑i,j​Pi,j​logPi,j​ on the nonnegative orthant, extended by +∞+\infty+∞ outside it, one obtains BΦ(P∣Q)=KL⁡(P∣Q)B_\Phi(\P\mid Q)=\operatorname{KL}(\P\mid Q)BΦ​(P∣Q)=KL(P∣Q). For P≥0\P\geq0P≥0 and Q>0Q>0Q>0, this identity is understood through the lower-semicontinuous extension, with 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0.

Bregman divergences are useful because their geometry can encode constraints. A Legendre-type generator blows up, or has an infinite derivative, at the boundary of its domain. For negative entropy, positivity is therefore built into the divergence, so one projects onto affine marginal constraints without separately handling non-negativity.

Linear Tilts and Gibbs References¶

Adding a linear cost to a Bregman penalty merely shifts the reference point in dual coordinates. The usual Gibbs--KL reformulation is exactly the entropy specialization.

Proposition: Linear Tilts of Bregman Penalties

Let Φ\PhiΦ be differentiable and strictly convex, and let BΦB_\PhiBΦ​ be its Bregman divergence. Fix a reference point QQQ in the interior of the domain. Assume that there exists QCQ^CQC such that

∇Φ(QC)=∇Φ(Q)−C/ϵ.\nabla\Phi(Q^C)=\nabla\Phi(Q)-C/\epsilon .∇Φ(QC)=∇Φ(Q)−C/ϵ.
(2)

Then, for all P\PP in the domain,

⟨P,C⟩+ϵBΦ(P∣Q)=ϵBΦ(P∣QC)+cst,\langle \P,C\rangle+\epsilon B_\Phi(\P\mid Q) = \epsilon B_\Phi(\P\mid Q^C)+\text{cst},⟨P,C⟩+ϵBΦ​(P∣Q)=ϵBΦ​(P∣QC)+cst,
(3)

where the constant does not depend on P\PP.

Proof

Subtract the two Bregman divergences:

BΦ(P∣QC)−BΦ(P∣Q)=⟨∇Φ(Q)−∇Φ(QC),P⟩+cst.B_\Phi(\P\mid Q^C)-B_\Phi(\P\mid Q) = \langle \nabla\Phi(Q)-\nabla\Phi(Q^C),\P\rangle+\text{cst}.BΦ​(P∣QC)−BΦ​(P∣Q)=⟨∇Φ(Q)−∇Φ(QC),P⟩+cst.
(4)

Using ∇Φ(Q)−∇Φ(QC)=C/ϵ\nabla\Phi(Q)-\nabla\Phi(Q^C)=C/\epsilon∇Φ(Q)−∇Φ(QC)=C/ϵ and multiplying by ϵ\epsilonϵ gives the claim.

For the negative entropy, take Q=a⊗bQ=a\otimes bQ=a⊗b. The tilted reference is

Ka,bϵ:=(a⊗b)⊙e−C/ϵ.K_{a,b}^\epsilon \eqdef (a\otimes b)\odot e^{-C/\epsilon}.Ka,bϵ​:=(a⊗b)⊙e−C/ϵ.
(5)

Thus

⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL⁡(P∣a⊗b)=ϵKL⁡(P∣Ka,bϵ)+cst.\langle \P,C\rangle+\epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\P\mid a\otimes b) = \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\P\mid K_{a,b}^\epsilon)+\text{cst}.⟨P,C⟩+ϵKL(P∣a⊗b)=ϵKL(P∣Ka,bϵ​)+cst.
(6)

On the transport polytope, scaling Ka,bϵK_{a,b}^\epsilonKa,bϵ​ is equivalent to scaling the Gibbs kernel K=e−C/ϵK=e^{-C/\epsilon}K=e−C/ϵ because the factors aia_iai​ and bjb_jbj​ can be absorbed into the Sinkhorn scalings. The unique entropic optimizer is the KL projection of this tilted Gibbs reference onto the coupling constraints:

Pϵ=arg min⁡P∈U(a,b)KL⁡(P∣Ka,bϵ).\P_\epsilon = \argmin_{\P\in\mathcal U(a,b)} \operatorname{KL}(\P\mid K_{a,b}^\epsilon).Pϵ​=P∈U(a,b)argmin​KL(P∣Ka,bϵ​).
(7)

Cyclic Projection Convergence¶

Given two closed convex constraint sets C1\mathcal C_1C1​ and C2\mathcal C_2C2​, the cyclic method projects first onto C1\mathcal C_1C1​, then onto C2\mathcal C_2C2​, and repeats. Full iterates satisfy the second constraint and half-iterates satisfy the first; both are attained together only in the limit.

The following algorithm records the general cyclic iteration. The two nonnegative constraint defects vanish on their respective sets and provide a practical stopping test.

Algorithm: Cyclic Bregman Projections

Input: Closed convex sets C1,C2\mathcal C_1,\mathcal C_2C1​,C2​, Bregman divergence BΦB_\PhiBΦ​, interior point P(0)\P^{(0)}P(0), constraint defects defC1,defC2\mathrm{def}_{\mathcal C_1},\mathrm{def}_{\mathcal C_2}defC1​​,defC2​​, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol, and iteration budget L≥1L\geq1L≥1.

Output: Approximate point in C1∩C2\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2C1​∩C2​ when the intersection is nonempty.

Initialize: Set r(0)=+∞r^{(0)}=+\inftyr(0)=+∞ and ℓ=0\ell=0ℓ=0.

While r(ℓ)>tolr^{(\ell)}>\mathrm{tol}r(ℓ)>tol and ℓ<L\ell<Lℓ<L do:

Set ℓ←ℓ+1\ell\leftarrow\ell+1ℓ←ℓ+1.

P(ℓ−1/2)=Proj⁡C1BΦ(P(ℓ−1))\P^{(\ell-1/2)}= \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_1}^{B_\Phi}(\P^{(\ell-1)})P(ℓ−1/2)=ProjC1​BΦ​​(P(ℓ−1)) and P(ℓ)=Proj⁡C2BΦ(P(ℓ−1/2))\P^{(\ell)}= \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_2}^{B_\Phi}(\P^{(\ell-1/2)})P(ℓ)=ProjC2​BΦ​​(P(ℓ−1/2)).

Set r(ℓ)=max⁡{defC1(P(ℓ)),defC2(P(ℓ))}r^{(\ell)}=\max\{\mathrm{def}_{\mathcal C_1}(\P^{(\ell)}), \mathrm{def}_{\mathcal C_2}(\P^{(\ell)})\}r(ℓ)=max{defC1​​(P(ℓ)),defC2​​(P(ℓ))}.

Return P(ℓ)\P^{(\ell)}P(ℓ).

The convergence mechanism is the classical one of Bregman projections Bregman, 1967. General convex constraints determine a feasible limit, while affine constraints give the stronger closest-point characterization.

Proposition: Convergence of Cyclic Bregman Projections

Let Φ\PhiΦ be a Legendre generator on a finite-dimensional convex domain, and let C1,C2\mathcal C_1,\mathcal C_2C1​,C2​ be closed convex sets whose intersection meets the interior of the domain. Generate (P(ℓ−1/2),P(ℓ))(\P^{(\ell-1/2)},\P^{(\ell)})(P(ℓ−1/2),P(ℓ)) with Algorithm: Cyclic Bregman Projections from an interior point P(0)\P^{(0)}P(0). Assume that the projections are well-defined and that all half-steps remain in a compact subset of the interior. Then there exists Pˉ∈C1∩C2\bar\P\in\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2Pˉ∈C1​∩C2​ such that P(ℓ)→Pˉ\P^{(\ell)}\to\bar\PP(ℓ)→Pˉ and P(ℓ−1/2)→Pˉ\P^{(\ell-1/2)}\to\bar\PP(ℓ−1/2)→Pˉ.

If, in addition, C1\mathcal C_1C1​ and C2\mathcal C_2C2​ are affine, then

Pˉ=Proj⁡C1∩C2BΦ(P(0)).\bar\P = \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2}^{B_\Phi}(\P^{(0)}).Pˉ=ProjC1​∩C2​BΦ​​(P(0)).
(8)
Proof

For three interior points, the Bregman three-point formula is

BΦ(Q∣P)=BΦ(Q∣P+)+BΦ(P+∣P)+⟨∇Φ(P+)−∇Φ(P),Q−P+⟩.B_\Phi(Q\mid\P) = B_\Phi(Q\mid\P^+) +B_\Phi(\P^+\mid\P) +\langle\nabla\Phi(\P^+)-\nabla\Phi(\P),Q-\P^+\rangle .BΦ​(Q∣P)=BΦ​(Q∣P+)+BΦ​(P+∣P)+⟨∇Φ(P+)−∇Φ(P),Q−P+⟩.
(9)

If P+=Proj⁡CBΦ(P)\P^+=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C}^{B_\Phi}(\P)P+=ProjCBΦ​​(P) and C\mathcal CC is closed and convex, first-order optimality gives

⟨∇Φ(P+)−∇Φ(P),Q−P+⟩≥0(Q∈C).\langle\nabla\Phi(\P^+)-\nabla\Phi(\P),Q-\P^+\rangle\geq0 \qquad (Q\in\mathcal C).⟨∇Φ(P+)−∇Φ(P),Q−P+⟩≥0(Q∈C).
(10)

Consequently,

BΦ(Q∣P)≥BΦ(Q∣P+)+BΦ(P+∣P).B_\Phi(Q\mid\P) \geq B_\Phi(Q\mid\P^+)+B_\Phi(\P^+\mid\P).BΦ​(Q∣P)≥BΦ​(Q∣P+)+BΦ​(P+∣P).
(11)

Let Z(2ℓ)=P(ℓ)Z^{(2\ell)}=\P^{(\ell)}Z(2ℓ)=P(ℓ) and Z(2ℓ+1)=P(ℓ+1/2)Z^{(2\ell+1)}=\P^{(\ell+1/2)}Z(2ℓ+1)=P(ℓ+1/2). For every Q∈C1∩C2Q\in\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2Q∈C1​∩C2​, applying this inequality at each half-step shows that BΦ(Q∣Z(r))B_\Phi(Q\mid Z^{(r)})BΦ​(Q∣Z(r)) decreases and that ∑rBΦ(Z(r+1)∣Z(r))<+∞\sum_r B_\Phi(Z^{(r+1)}\mid Z^{(r)})<+\infty∑r​BΦ​(Z(r+1)∣Z(r))<+∞. Compactness and strict convexity imply ∥Z(r+1)−Z(r)∥→0\|Z^{(r+1)}-Z^{(r)}\|\to0∥Z(r+1)−Z(r)∥→0. Hence every cluster point belongs to both closed sets. If Pˉ\bar\PPˉ is one such point, then BΦ(Pˉ∣Z(r))B_\Phi(\bar\P\mid Z^{(r)})BΦ​(Pˉ∣Z(r)) decreases to zero along a subsequence and therefore along the whole sequence. Thus Z(r)→PˉZ^{(r)}\to\bar\PZ(r)→Pˉ.

For affine sets the first-order inequality is an equality. The dual displacements at successive half-steps lie in the two fixed normal spaces; telescoping gives

∇Φ(Pˉ)−∇Φ(P(0))∈NC1+NC2=NC1∩C2.\nabla\Phi(\bar\P)-\nabla\Phi(\P^{(0)}) \in N_{\mathcal C_1}+N_{\mathcal C_2} = N_{\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2}.∇Φ(Pˉ)−∇Φ(P(0))∈NC1​​+NC2​​=NC1​∩C2​​.
(12)

This is the optimality condition for the displayed Bregman projection onto the intersection.

Row and Column Scalings¶

We now apply the general Bregman-projection framework to entropic OT. The two affine constraints impose the source and target marginals, while negative entropy turns their cyclic projections into explicit row and column rescalings. Denote these constraint sets by

Ca1:={P∈Rn×m:P1m=a},Cb2:={P∈Rn×m:P⊤1n=b}.\mathcal C_a^1 \eqdef \{\P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}:\P\mathbf 1_m=a\}, \qquad \mathcal C_b^2 \eqdef \{\P\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}:\P^\top\mathbf 1_n=b\}.Ca1​:={P∈Rn×m:P1m​=a},Cb2​:={P∈Rn×m:P⊤1n​=b}.
(13)

Positivity is a separate constraint, so

U(a,b)=Ca1∩Cb2∩R+n×m.\mathcal U(a,b) = \mathcal C_a^1\cap\mathcal C_b^2\cap\mathbb R_+^{n\times m}.U(a,b)=Ca1​∩Cb2​∩R+n×m​.
(14)

For negative entropy, however, the Legendre generator has effective domain Ω=R+n×m\Omega=\mathbb R_+^{n\times m}Ω=R+n×m​ and is +∞+\infty+∞ outside Ω\OmegaΩ. Thus Proj⁡CiKL⁡\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_i}^{\operatorname{KL}}ProjCi​KL​ already minimizes over Ci∩Ω\mathcal C_i\cap\OmegaCi​∩Ω: the generator enforces positivity, which need not be repeated in the projector notation. The cyclic iteration therefore specializes to

P(2ℓ+1)=Proj⁡Ca1KL⁡(P(2ℓ)),P(2ℓ+2)=Proj⁡Cb2KL⁡(P(2ℓ+1)).\P^{(2\ell+1)} = \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_a^1}^{\operatorname{KL}}(\P^{(2\ell)}), \qquad \P^{(2\ell+2)} = \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_b^2}^{\operatorname{KL}}(\P^{(2\ell+1)}).P(2ℓ+1)=ProjCa1​KL​(P(2ℓ)),P(2ℓ+2)=ProjCb2​KL​(P(2ℓ+1)).
(15)

These two projectors are explicit: they rescale respectively the rows and the columns.

Proposition: KL Projections are Scalings

One has

Proj⁡Ca1KL⁡(P)=diag⁡ ⁣(aP1m)P,Proj⁡Cb2KL⁡(P)=Pdiag⁡ ⁣(bP⊤1n).\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_a^1}^{\operatorname{KL}}(\P) = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{a}{\P\mathbf 1_m}\right)\P, \qquad \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_b^2}^{\operatorname{KL}}(\P) = \P\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{b}{\P^\top\mathbf 1_n}\right).ProjCa1​KL​(P)=diag(P1m​a​)P,ProjCb2​KL​(P)=Pdiag(P⊤1n​b​).
(16)
Proof

Along each row or column vector, impose a fixed sum s>0s>0s>0:

min⁡p{KL⁡(p∣q):⟨p,1⟩=s}.\min_p \left\{ \operatorname{KL}(p\mid q) : \langle p,\mathbf 1\rangle=s \right\}.pmin​{KL(p∣q):⟨p,1⟩=s}.
(17)

The Lagrange multiplier equation gives log⁡(p/q)+λ1=0\log(p/q)+\lambda\mathbf 1=0log(p/q)+λ1=0, hence p=uqp=uqp=uq with u=e−λ>0u=e^{-\lambda}>0u=e−λ>0. The constraint fixes u=s/∑iqiu=s/\sum_i q_iu=s/∑i​qi​, which is exactly the scaling formula.

For positive histograms and a strictly positive Gibbs kernel, iterative proportional fitting keeps the half-steps positive and converges Ruschendorf, 1995Rüschendorf & Thomsen, 1998. Since the two marginal sets are affine, Proposition: Convergence of Cyclic Bregman Projections, applied with P(0)=Ka,bϵ\P^{(0)}=K_{a,b}^\epsilonP(0)=Ka,bϵ​, identifies the limit as the entropic optimizer.

Defining

P(2ℓ):=diag⁡(u(ℓ))Kdiag⁡(v(ℓ)),\P^{(2\ell)} \eqdef \operatorname{diag}(u^{(\ell)})K\operatorname{diag}(v^{(\ell)}),P(2ℓ):=diag(u(ℓ))Kdiag(v(ℓ)),
(18)

the two projection steps are the usual Sinkhorn updates on the scaling vectors. In practice one stores the vectors and multiplies by the Gibbs kernel, often exploiting separable, sparse, low-rank or geometric structure.

The Bregman proof is geometric, but its direct finite-dimensional linear-rate constants can degrade with dimension and with small ϵ\epsilonϵ. The robust dual analysis below gives a dimension-free qualitative message: before any local linear regime becomes visible, one can still guarantee an O(1/ℓ)O(1/\ell)O(1/ℓ) dual gap whose constants depend on the cost range and potential oscillation.

Other Divergences¶

The simplicity of the KL construction relies on negative entropy encoding nonnegativity through its effective domain. Suppose instead that Φ\PhiΦ is Legendre on the full space Rn×m\mathbb R^{n\times m}Rn×m. Positivity must then be included explicitly in the marginal constraints:

Ca,+1:=Ca1∩R+n×m,Cb,+2:=Cb2∩R+n×m.\mathcal C_{a,+}^1 \eqdef \mathcal C_a^1\cap\mathbb R_+^{n\times m}, \qquad \mathcal C_{b,+}^2 \eqdef \mathcal C_b^2\cap\mathbb R_+^{n\times m}.Ca,+1​:=Ca1​∩R+n×m​,Cb,+2​:=Cb2​∩R+n×m​.
(19)

Thus U(a,b)=Ca,+1∩Cb,+2\mathcal U(a,b)=\mathcal C_{a,+}^1\cap\mathcal C_{b,+}^2U(a,b)=Ca,+1​∩Cb,+2​. These sets are convex but no longer affine, and their BΦB_\PhiBΦ​-projectors generally have no closed-form scaling formula. The affine clause of Proposition: Convergence of Cyclic Bregman Projections no longer applies: ordinary cyclic projections may converge to a feasible point without computing Proj⁡U(a,b)BΦ(P(0))\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal U(a,b)}^{B_\Phi}(\P^{(0)})ProjU(a,b)BΦ​​(P(0)).

For the Euclidean generator Φ(P)=12∥P∥F2\Phi(\P)=\frac12\|\P\|_{\mathrm F}^2Φ(P)=21​∥P∥F2​, projection onto Ca,+1\mathcal C_{a,+}^1Ca,+1​ is a rowwise simplex projection:

[Proj⁡Ca,+1BΦ(Q)]i,j=(Qi,j−τi)+,∑j(Qi,j−τi)+=ai.\left[ \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_{a,+}^1}^{B_\Phi}(Q) \right]_{i,j} = (Q_{i,j}-\tau_i)_+, \qquad \sum_j(Q_{i,j}-\tau_i)_+=a_i.[ProjCa,+1​BΦ​​(Q)]i,j​=(Qi,j​−τi​)+​,j∑​(Qi,j​−τi​)+​=ai​.
(20)

The column formula is analogous. These thresholds are not multiplicative scalings, but sorting or selection computes them efficiently Blondel et al., 2018.

To recover the closest-point projection onto the intersection, Dykstra’s algorithm alternates the same Bregman projectors while carrying correction variables in dual coordinates. Under the standard finite-dimensional assumptions, it converges to Proj⁡Ca,+1∩Cb,+2BΦ(P(0))\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathcal C_{a,+}^1\cap\mathcal C_{b,+}^2}^{B_\Phi} (\P^{(0)})ProjCa,+1​∩Cb,+2​BΦ​​(P(0)) Dykstra, 1985Censor & Reich, 1998Bauschke & Lewis, 2000. Benamou, Carlier, Cuturi, Nenna, and Peyré developed this construction systematically for regularized transport Benamou et al., 2015. Through Fenchel duality, Bregman--Dykstra is block-coordinate ascent on the marginal dual potentials; the correction variables store the dual memory absent from plain cyclic projection Bregman et al., 1999.

For the quadratic generator and the product reference ξ=a⊗b\xi=a\otimes bξ=a⊗b,

BΦ(P∣ξ)=12∑i,j(Pi,j−aibj)2.B_\Phi(\P\mid\xi) = \frac12\sum_{i,j}(\P_{i,j}-a_i b_j)^2.BΦ​(P∣ξ)=21​i,j∑​(Pi,j​−ai​bj​)2.
(21)

This is closely related, but not identical, to the quadratic ϕ\phiϕ-divergence generated by ϕ(r)=12(r−1)2\phi(r)=\frac12(r-1)^2ϕ(r)=21​(r−1)2:

Dϕ(P∣a⊗b)=12∑i,j(Pi,j−aibj)2aibj,D_\phi(\P\mid a\otimes b) = \frac12\sum_{i,j}\frac{(\P_{i,j}-a_i b_j)^2}{a_i b_j},Dϕ​(P∣a⊗b)=21​i,j∑​ai​bj​(Pi,j​−ai​bj​)2​,
(22)

for positive ai,bja_i,b_jai​,bj​. The difference is the fixed inverse product-marginal weighting in the second quadratic norm. Both models yield positive-part thresholding and potentially sparse plans. The section on Other Convex Regularizers develops their dual laws and alternating dual-maximization algorithms.

Sinkhorn Convergence: Monotone Point of View¶

This section isolates the order structure shared by generalized Sinkhorn updates. It first introduces the abstract language of topical maps, then applies it to the generalized soft transforms of Other Convex Regularizers, and finally derives a monotone fixed-point argument valid beyond KL regularization.

Variation Seminorm and Topical Maps¶

Potentials are defined only up to additive constants, so their natural gauge-invariant size is their oscillation.

Definition: Variation Seminorm

For a bounded real-valued function hhh, define

∥h∥V:=sup⁡h−inf⁡h.\norm{h}_V \eqdef \sup h-\inf h.∥h∥V​:=suph−infh.
(23)

It vanishes exactly on constant functions and therefore induces a norm after quotienting by additive constants.

The order maps relevant to Sinkhorn commute with this additive gauge.

Definition: Topical Map

Let EEE be an ordered vector space of functions containing the constants. A map T:E→E\mathcal T:E\to ET:E→E is topical if

f≤g⟹T(f)≤T(g),T(f+s)=T(f)+s(s∈R).f\leq g\Longrightarrow\mathcal T(f)\leq\mathcal T(g), \qquad \mathcal T(f+s)=\mathcal T(f)+s \quad(s\in\mathbb R).f≤g⟹T(f)≤T(g),T(f+s)=T(f)+s(s∈R).
(24)
Proposition: Topical Maps are Variation-Nonexpansive

Every topical map on a vector space of bounded real-valued functions satisfies

∥T(f)−T(g)∥V≤∥f−g∥V.\norm{\mathcal T(f)-\mathcal T(g)}_V \leq \norm{f-g}_V.∥T(f)−T(g)∥V​≤∥f−g∥V​.
(25)

The same conclusion holds if T\mathcal TT is order reversing and additively anti-homogeneous: T(f+s)=T(f)−s\mathcal T(f+s)=\mathcal T(f)-sT(f+s)=T(f)−s.

Thus the oscillation of T(f)−T(g)\mathcal T(f)-\mathcal T(g)T(f)−T(g) is at most b−a=∥f−g∥Vb-a=\norm{f-g}_Vb−a=∥f−g∥V​. In the order-reversing case, the corresponding interval is [−b,−a][-b,-a][−b,−a] and has the same length.

Remark: Topical Maps and Projective Geometry

Order-preserving additively homogeneous maps are called topical maps in nonlinear Perron--Frobenius theory Lemmens & Nussbaum, 2012. Proposition Proposition: Topical Maps are Variation-Nonexpansive is the additive counterpart of projective nonexpansiveness.

Generalized Sinkhorn Maps¶

For the ϕ\phiϕ-divergence regularized transport problem, the one-sided block updates are expressed using the Legendre transform ϕ∗\phi^*ϕ∗ defined in (47). They are the generalized soft ccc-transforms of (121), and their alternating dual-maximization scheme is (124). After choosing a consistent extremal minimizer whenever a scalar update is not unique, one full cycle acting on the first potential is

Aϕ(f):=(fc,ϵ,ϕ)cˉ,ϵ,ϕ.\mathcal A_\phi(f) \eqdef \big(f^{c,\epsilon,\phi}\big)^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}.Aϕ​(f):=(fc,ϵ,ϕ)cˉ,ϵ,ϕ.
(27)

For the KL generator, this is the usual double Sinkhorn map.

Proposition: Generalized Sinkhorn Maps are Topical

Assume that the scalar minimizer sets in (121) are nonempty compact intervals, and select either their smallest elements everywhere or their largest elements everywhere. Each selected one-sided transform is order reversing and additively anti-homogeneous:

g≤g′⟹gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ≥g′cˉ,ϵ,ϕ,(g+s)cˉ,ϵ,ϕ=gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ−s,g\leq g' \Longrightarrow g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}\geq {g'}^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}, \qquad (g+s)^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi} = g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}-s,g≤g′⟹gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ≥g′cˉ,ϵ,ϕ,(g+s)cˉ,ϵ,ϕ=gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ−s,
(28)

and likewise for f↦fc,ϵ,ϕf\mapsto f^{c,\epsilon,\phi}f↦fc,ϵ,ϕ. Consequently, Aϕ\mathcal A_\phiAϕ​ is topical and

∥Aϕ(f)−Aϕ(h)∥V≤∥f−h∥V.\norm{\mathcal A_\phi(f)-\mathcal A_\phi(h)}_V \leq \norm{f-h}_V.∥Aϕ​(f)−Aϕ​(h)∥V​≤∥f−h∥V​.
(29)

No selection convention is needed when the scalar minimizers are unique.

Proof

Since ϕ\phiϕ is extended by +∞+\infty+∞ on (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0), its Legendre transform ϕ∗\phi^*ϕ∗ from (47) is convex and nondecreasing. For fixed xxx, let Hgx(u)H_g^x(u)Hgx​(u) denote the scalar objective in the first line of (121). If g≤g′g\leq g'g≤g′, then u↦Hg′x(u)−Hgx(u)u\mapsto H_{g'}^x(u)-H_g^x(u)u↦Hg′x​(u)−Hgx​(u) is nondecreasing because s↦ϕ∗(s+δ)−ϕ∗(s)s\mapsto\phi^*(s+\delta)-\phi^*(s)s↦ϕ∗(s+δ)−ϕ∗(s) is nondecreasing for every δ≥0\delta\geq0δ≥0.

Let I=argmin⁡HgxI=\operatorname*{argmin}H_g^xI=argminHgx​ and I′=argmin⁡Hg′xI'=\operatorname*{argmin}H_{g'}^xI′=argminHg′x​. Comparing the two optimality inequalities shows that min⁡I′≤min⁡I\min I'\leq\min IminI′≤minI; the same argument gives max⁡I′≤max⁡I\max I'\leq\max ImaxI′≤maxI. Finally, Hg+sx(u)=Hgx(u+s)+sH_{g+s}^x(u)=H_g^x(u+s)+sHg+sx​(u)=Hgx​(u+s)+s, so either extremal selection is additively anti-homogeneous. The second one-sided transform is symmetric. Their composition is topical, and Proposition: Topical Maps are Variation-Nonexpansive gives the final estimate.

Topicality gives nonexpansiveness, not a strict contraction. For KL, positivity of the Gibbs kernel supplies the stronger Hilbert-metric contraction proved in Sinkhorn Convergence: Linear Hilbert Metric Rate; no comparable strict factor follows from the order properties alone for a general ϕ\phiϕ.

Monotone Convergence for Generalized Sinkhorn¶

The following order argument traces back to Fortet’s proof of the Schrodinger system Fortet, 1940Essid & Pavon, 2019Léonard, 2019. It is not based on an optimization principle: a subsolution generates an increasing orbit, while a fixed point provides an upper barrier.

Proposition: Monotone Convergence of Generalized Sinkhorn Cycles

Let X\mathcal XX and Y\mathcal YY be compact metric spaces and c∈C(X×Y)c\in C(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)c∈C(X×Y). Suppose that the assumptions of Proposition: Generalized Sinkhorn Maps are Topical hold, that the selected transforms are finite valued, and that Aϕ\mathcal A_\phiAϕ​ has a fixed point f⋆∈C(X)f^\star\in C(\mathcal X)f⋆∈C(X).

If f(0)∈C(X)f^{(0)}\in C(\mathcal X)f(0)∈C(X) is a subsolution, f(0)≤Aϕ(f(0))f^{(0)}\leq\mathcal A_\phi(f^{(0)})f(0)≤Aϕ​(f(0)), then

f(ℓ+1)=Aϕ(f(ℓ))f^{(\ell+1)} = \mathcal A_\phi(f^{(\ell)})f(ℓ+1)=Aϕ​(f(ℓ))
(30)

converges uniformly to a fixed point of Aϕ\mathcal A_\phiAϕ​. The analogous conclusion holds for a supersolution, with a decreasing sequence. If the fixed point is unique modulo additive constants, the corresponding potential classes converge to this unique class.

Proof

Because Aϕ\mathcal A_\phiAϕ​ is additively homogeneous, shifting a subsolution preserves its defining inequality. Shift it below a fixed point. Topicality then gives

f(0)≤f(1)≤⋯≤f⋆,f^{(0)} \leq f^{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq f^\star,f(0)≤f(1)≤⋯≤f⋆,
(31)

so the orbit converges pointwise.

The one-sided transforms inherit the modulus of continuity of the cost. If δ(x,x′)=sup⁡y∣c(x,y)−c(x′,y)∣\delta(x,x')=\sup_y|c(x,y)-c(x',y)|δ(x,x′)=supy​∣c(x,y)−c(x′,y)∣, then order reversal and additive anti-homogeneity give

∣gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x)−gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x′)∣≤δ(x,x′).\left| g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}(x) - g^{\bar c,\epsilon,\phi}(x') \right| \leq \delta(x,x').∣∣​gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x)−gcˉ,ϵ,ϕ(x′)∣∣​≤δ(x,x′).
(32)

The orbit is therefore uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Arzela--Ascoli upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence. The same order and shift properties also make each one-sided transform nonexpansive in the uniform norm, so Aϕ\mathcal A_\phiAϕ​ is continuous and the limit is a fixed point. The supersolution argument reverses all inequalities.

The subsolution and supersolution conditions are invariant under additive shifts, but a shift cannot turn an arbitrary initialization into either one. The proposition therefore isolates the genuinely order-theoretic convergence mechanism; unrestricted initialization requires an additional compactness, ascent, or contraction argument.

Sinkhorn Convergence: Sublinear Robust Rate¶

The preceding projection and monotonicity arguments establish convergence but do not provide a quantitative rate. The Hilbert-metric analysis in Sinkhorn Convergence: Linear Hilbert Metric Rate will give geometric, or linear, convergence, the canonical asymptotic behavior of a strictly contractive fixed-point iteration; however, the gap between its global contraction factor and one typically becomes exponentially small in the cost oscillation divided by ϵ\epsilonϵ. We therefore first establish a slower O(1/ℓ)O(1/\ell)O(1/ℓ) dual-gap rate whose constant grows only as 1/ϵ1/\epsilon1/ϵ Peyré, 2026Altschuler et al., 2017Dvurechensky et al., 2018. This robust dependence is crucial when Sinkhorn approximates unregularized discrete OT: Corollary Corollary: Approximating Unregularized OT by Regularized Dual Costs chooses ϵ=δ/(2log⁡(nm))\epsilon=\delta/(2\log(nm))ϵ=δ/(2log(nm)), so the temperature decreases with the requested accuracy and with the number of support points.

Sinkhorn Convergence: Linear Hilbert Metric Rate¶

Hilbert’s projective metric measures positive scaling vectors modulo global multiplication. A positive kernel contracts this geometry, yielding a global linear rate for Sinkhorn scaling rays.

Projective Contraction¶

Definition: Hilbert Metric

For u,u′∈R+,∗nu,u'\in\RR_{+,*}^nu,u′∈R+,∗n​, define

H(u,u′):=∥log⁡u−log⁡u′∥V.\mathsf H(u,u') \eqdef \norm{\log u-\log u'}_V.H(u,u′):=∥logu−logu′∥V​.
(44)

Here, ∥⋅∥V\norm{\cdot}_V∥⋅∥V​ is the variation seminorm of Definition Definition: Variation Seminorm, specialized to functions on the finite space {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}: ∥z∥V=max⁡izi−min⁡izi\norm z_V=\max_i z_i-\min_i z_i∥z∥V​=maxi​zi​−mini​zi​.

Multiplying either vector by a positive scalar leaves H\mathsf HH unchanged. It is therefore a metric only on projective classes.

Proposition: Hilbert Metric on the Projective Cone

The function H\mathsf HH defines a complete metric on R+,∗n/ ⁣∼\RR_{+,*}^n/\!\simR+,∗n​/∼, where u∼u′u\sim u'u∼u′ when u=su′u=su'u=su′ for some s>0s>0s>0.

Proof

The logarithm identifies the projective cone with Rn/span⁡(1n)\RR^n/\operatorname{span}(\mathbf1_n)Rn/span(1n​). The variation seminorm vanishes exactly on constant vectors, hence induces a norm on this quotient. Completeness follows from finite dimensionality.

Theorem: Birkhoff Contraction Theorem

Let K∈R+,∗n×mK\in\RR_{+,*}^{n\times m}K∈R+,∗n×m​. Then

H(Kv,Kv′)≤λ(K)H(v,v′),\mathsf H(Kv,Kv') \leq \lambda(K)\mathsf H(v,v'),H(Kv,Kv′)≤λ(K)H(v,v′),
(45)

where

λ(K):=η(K)−1η(K)+1<1,η(K):=max⁡i,j,k,ℓKi,kKj,ℓKj,kKi,ℓ.\lambda(K) \eqdef \frac{\sqrt{\eta(K)}-1}{\sqrt{\eta(K)}+1}<1, \qquad \eta(K) \eqdef \max_{i,j,k,\ell} \frac{K_{i,k}K_{j,\ell}}{K_{j,k}K_{i,\ell}}.λ(K):=η(K)​+1η(K)​−1​<1,η(K):=i,j,k,ℓmax​Kj,k​Ki,ℓ​Ki,k​Kj,ℓ​​.
(46)
Proof

The Birkhoff--Hopf theorem contracts Hilbert’s metric by tanh⁡(Δ(A)/4)\tanh(\Delta(A)/4)tanh(Δ(A)/4), where Δ(A)=sup⁡u,v>0H(Au,Av)\Delta(A)=\sup_{u,v>0}\mathsf H(Au,Av)Δ(A)=supu,v>0​H(Au,Av) is the projective diameter. For a positive matrix, output cross-ratios give Δ(K)=log⁡η(K)\Delta(K)=\log\eta(K)Δ(K)=logη(K). Hence tanh⁡(Δ(K)/4)=(η(K)−1)/(η(K)+1)\tanh(\Delta(K)/4)=(\sqrt{\eta(K)}-1)/(\sqrt{\eta(K)}+1)tanh(Δ(K)/4)=(η(K)​−1)/(η(K)​+1) Birkhoff, 1957.

The theorem applies to positive linear maps between proper cones. Related nonlinear projective results require order preservation and homogeneity; a generic affine map is not covered.

Theorem: Projective Linear Convergence of Sinkhorn

Let v(0)>0v^{(0)}>0v(0)>0, generate Sinkhorn iterates, and fix optimal scalings (u⋆,v⋆)(u^\star,v^\star)(u⋆,v⋆). For ℓ≥1\ell\geq1ℓ≥1, set

H(u(ℓ),u⋆)≤H(P(ℓ)1m,a)1−λ2,ℓ≥1,\mathsf H(u^{(\ell)},u^\star) \leq \frac{\mathsf H(\P^{(\ell)}\mathbf1_m,a)}{1-\lambda^2}, \qquad \ell\geq1,H(u(ℓ),u⋆)≤1−λ2H(P(ℓ)1m​,a)​,ℓ≥1,
(55)

and

H(v(ℓ),v⋆)≤H((P(ℓ+1/2))⊤1n,b)1−λ2,ℓ≥0.\mathsf H(v^{(\ell)},v^\star) \leq \frac{\mathsf H((\P^{(\ell+1/2)})^\top\mathbf1_n,b)}{1-\lambda^2}, \qquad \ell\geq0.H(v(ℓ),v⋆)≤1−λ2H((P(ℓ+1/2))⊤1n​,b)​,ℓ≥0.

Finally,

∥log⁡P(ℓ)−log⁡P⋆∥∞≤H(u(ℓ),u⋆)+H(v(ℓ),v⋆).\norm{\log \P^{(\ell)}-\log \P^\star}_\infty \leq \mathsf H(u^{(\ell)},u^\star) + \mathsf H(v^{(\ell)},v^\star).∥∥​logP(ℓ)−logP⋆∥∥​∞​≤H(u(ℓ),u⋆)+H(v(ℓ),v⋆).
(57)
Proof

Entrywise multiplication by a fixed positive vector and entrywise inversion are isometries of Hilbert’s metric. The row map R(v)=a/(Kv)R(v)=a/(Kv)R(v)=a/(Kv) and column map C(u)=b/(K⊤u)C(u)=b/(K^\top u)C(u)=b/(K⊤u) are therefore both λ\lambdaλ-Lipschitz. The full-cycle maps C∘RC\circ RC∘R and R∘CR\circ CR∘C contract by λ2\lambda^2λ2, which gives the first bounds.

For a qqq-contraction FFF with fixed point x⋆x^\starx⋆,

d(x,x⋆)≤d(x,Fx)1−q.d(x,x^\star) \leq \frac{d(x,Fx)}{1-q}.d(x,x⋆)≤1−qd(x,Fx)​.
(58)

Applying this with q=λ2q=\lambda^2q=λ2 and using

H(u(ℓ+1),u(ℓ))=H(a,P(ℓ)1m),\mathsf H(u^{(\ell+1)},u^{(\ell)}) = \mathsf H(a,\P^{(\ell)}\mathbf1_m),H(u(ℓ+1),u(ℓ))=H(a,P(ℓ)1m​),
(59)
H(v(ℓ+1),v(ℓ))=H(b,(P(ℓ+1/2))⊤1n)\mathsf H(v^{(\ell+1)},v^{(\ell)}) = \mathsf H(b,(\P^{(\ell+1/2)})^\top\mathbf1_n)H(v(ℓ+1),v(ℓ))=H(b,(P(ℓ+1/2))⊤1n​)
(60)

gives the posterior estimates. For the plan bound, write ξi=log⁡(ui(ℓ)/ui⋆)\xi_i=\log(u_i^{(\ell)}/u_i^\star)ξi​=log(ui(ℓ)​/ui⋆​) and ζj=log⁡(vj(ℓ)/vj⋆)\zeta_j=\log(v_j^{(\ell)}/v_j^\star)ζj​=log(vj(ℓ)​/vj⋆​). Both plans have mass one, so zero lies between the minimum and maximum of ξ⊕ζ\xi\oplus\zetaξ⊕ζ; its sup norm is bounded by its oscillation, which is ∥ξ∥V+∥ζ∥V\norm\xi_V+\norm\zeta_V∥ξ∥V​+∥ζ∥V​.

Dual-Potential Form¶

The KL-normalized potentials satisfy fℓ=ϵlog⁡(u(ℓ)⊘a)f_\ell=\epsilon\log(u^{(\ell)}\oslash a)fℓ​=ϵlog(u(ℓ)⊘a) and gℓ=ϵlog⁡(v(ℓ)⊘b)g_\ell=\epsilon\log(v^{(\ell)}\oslash b)gℓ​=ϵlog(v(ℓ)⊘b). Hence

∥fℓ−f⋆∥V=ϵH(u(ℓ),u⋆),∥gℓ−g⋆∥V=ϵH(v(ℓ),v⋆).\norm{f_\ell-f^\star}_V = \epsilon\mathsf H(u^{(\ell)},u^\star), \qquad \norm{g_\ell-g^\star}_V = \epsilon\mathsf H(v^{(\ell)},v^\star).∥fℓ​−f⋆∥V​=ϵH(u(ℓ),u⋆),∥gℓ​−g⋆∥V​=ϵH(v(ℓ),v⋆).
(65)

The temperature factor is essential when passing to coupling densities:

∥log⁡( dπℓ/ dπ⋆)∥∞≤∥fℓ−f⋆∥V+∥gℓ−g⋆∥Vϵ.\norm{\log(\d\pi_\ell/\d\pi^\star)}_\infty \leq \frac{\norm{f_\ell-f^\star}_V+\norm{g_\ell-g^\star}_V}{\epsilon}.∥log(dπℓ​/dπ⋆)∥∞​≤ϵ∥fℓ​−f⋆∥V​+∥gℓ​−g⋆∥V​​.
(66)

For Kϵ=e−C/ϵK_\epsilon=e^{-C/\epsilon}Kϵ​=e−C/ϵ and R=max⁡C−min⁡CR=\max C-\min CR=maxC−minC,

λ(Kϵ)≤tanh⁡ ⁣(R2ϵ)<1.\lambda(K_\epsilon) \leq \tanh\!\left(\frac{R}{2\epsilon}\right)<1.λ(Kϵ​)≤tanh(2ϵR​)<1.
(67)

Thus the global rate becomes exponentially pessimistic as ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow0ϵ↓0. Sharper continuous analyses obtain polynomial rates under additional semiconcavity or log-concavity assumptions Chizat et al., 2026. In practice, monitor the marginal not just normalized: the source residual at P(ℓ)P^{(\ell)}P(ℓ) and the target residual at P(ℓ+1/2)P^{(\ell+1/2)}P(ℓ+1/2) are the two meaningful posterior diagnostics.

Entropic Optimal Transport Between Gaussians¶

Gaussian marginals provide an explicit finite-dimensional model of Sinkhorn’s behavior. The soft ccc-transform preserves quadratic potentials, the optimal entropic coupling is Gaussian, and the value can be written with matrix square roots Janati et al., 2020. This is the entropic counterpart of the Gaussian W2\Wass_2W2​ and Bures formula.

This scalar calculation illustrates the general Gaussian convergence picture of Chizat, Delalande and Vaskevicius Chizat et al., 2026: the rate improves when ϵ\epsilonϵ is large or the covariance scales overlap well, and deteriorates in the small-temperature limit where the entropic coupling approaches a deterministic Brenier map.

Continuous ε\varepsilonε-Sinkhorn Flow¶

This section studies a simultaneous high-resolution, many-iteration limit. It is not a continuous-time interpolation of a fixed-temperature algorithm: the grid is refined while the temperature and the fictitious time step both vanish as 1/k1/k1/k.

Parabolic Monge--Ampere Limit¶

For the quadratic torus cost c(x,y)=dTd(x,y)2/2c(x,y)=d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)^2/2c(x,y)=dTd​(x,y)2/2, Berman’s scaling discretizes both marginals on a grid of mesh 1/k1/k1/k, sets ϵk=1/k\epsilon_k=1/kϵk​=1/k, and assigns duration 1/k1/k1/k to each Sinkhorn update Berman, 2020. The mmm-th log-potential is observed at time t=m/kt=m/kt=m/k. In this coupled limit, Sinkhorn becomes a parabolic Monge--Ampere flow.

(89)

The multiplicative increment is

ρk,u(x):=ek(Sku(x)−u(x))=e−ku(x)∫e−kc(x,y)∫e−k(c(x′,y)+u(x′)) dα(k)(x′) dβ(k)(y).\rho_{k,u}(x) \eqdef e^{k(S_ku(x)-u(x))} = e^{-ku(x)} \int \frac{e^{-kc(x,y)}} {\int e^{-k(c(x',y)+u(x'))}\,d\alpha^{(k)}(x')} \,d\beta^{(k)}(y).ρk,u​(x):=ek(Sk​u(x)−u(x))=e−ku(x)∫∫e−k(c(x′,y)+u(x′))dα(k)(x′)e−kc(x,y)​dβ(k)(y).
(90)

The normalized update subtracts the spatial mean of SkuS_kuSk​u.

Proposition: Scaled Log-Sinkhorn Limit

Let ϵk=1/k\epsilon_k=1/kϵk​=1/k, generate the mean-zero grid iterates with SkS_kSk​, and set u(k)(t)=u⌊kt⌋(k)u^{(k)}(t)=u_{\lfloor kt\rfloor}^{(k)}u(k)(t)=u⌊kt⌋(k)​. Assume smooth convergence to utu_tut​ on compact time intervals, I+∇2ut≻0I+\nabla^2u_t\succ0I+∇2ut​≻0, and uniform validity of the Laplace expansion below. Then utu_tut​ solves the continuous ε\varepsilonε-Sinkhorn flow.

Proof

The normalized increment is

um+1(k)−um(k)=1k[log⁡ρk,um(k)−∫Tdlog⁡ρk,um(k) dx].u_{m+1}^{(k)}-u_m^{(k)} = \frac1k\left[ \log\rho_{k,u_m^{(k)}} - \int_{\mathbb T^d}\log\rho_{k,u_m^{(k)}}\,dx \right].um+1(k)​−um(k)​=k1​[logρk,um(k)​​−∫Td​logρk,um(k)​​dx].
(91)

Berman’s discrete Laplace estimate gives

ρk,u(x)=det⁡(I+∇2u(x))eF(x)−G(x+∇u(x))(1+O(k−1)).\rho_{k,u}(x) = \det(I+\nabla^2u(x)) e^{F(x)-G(x+\nabla u(x))} \bigl(1+O(k^{-1})\bigr).ρk,u​(x)=det(I+∇2u(x))eF(x)−G(x+∇u(x))(1+O(k−1)).
(92)

Taking logarithms, dividing by the time step 1/k1/k1/k, and passing to the smooth limit gives the stated PDE with its mean-zero gauge correction.

No explicit ϵ\epsilonϵ remains in the normalized limiting PDE: it records the vanishing temperature before rescaling. The Kahler analogue is the parabolic complex Monge--Ampere equation.

Proposition: Stationary Continuous Sinkhorn Potentials

Let uuu be a smooth stationary solution with I+∇2u≻0I+\nabla^2u\succ0I+∇2u≻0, and define T(x)=x+∇u(x)T(x)=x+\nabla u(x)T(x)=x+∇u(x) modulo Zd\mathbb Z^dZd. Then T#α=βT_{\#}\alpha=\betaT#​α=β. Conversely, any smooth map of this form with T#α=βT_{\#}\alpha=\betaT#​α=β solves the stationary equation up to the additive gauge of uuu.

Proof

At stationarity,

log⁡det⁡(I+∇2u(x))−G(T(x))+F(x)=c.\log\det(I+\nabla^2u(x))-G(T(x))+F(x)=c.logdet(I+∇2u(x))−G(T(x))+F(x)=c.
(93)

Hence

e−G(T(x))det⁡(∇T(x))=e−F(x)ec.e^{-G(T(x))}\det(\nabla T(x))=e^{-F(x)}e^c.e−G(T(x))det(∇T(x))=e−F(x)ec.
(94)

The positive-definite Jacobian makes TTT an orientation-preserving local diffeomorphism. Since it is homotopic to the identity, it has degree one and is a diffeomorphism of the torus. Both measures have mass one, so change of variables gives ec=1e^c=1ec=1. The identity is then exactly the Jacobian equation for T#α=βT_{\#}\alpha=\betaT#​α=β. The converse reverses the argument.

Gaussian Closure¶

Gaussian marginals give a finite-dimensional test case for the continuous flow. The theorem above is stated on the flat torus, but the same local Laplace calculation can be read formally on Rd\RR^dRd for confining Gaussian densities. Write α=N(mα,Σα)\alpha=\Gaussian(m_\alpha,\Sigma_\alpha)α=N(mα​,Σα​) and β=N(mβ,Σβ)\beta=\Gaussian(m_\beta,\Sigma_\beta)β=N(mβ​,Σβ​), and restrict the potential to the quadratic ansatz for which

Tt(x):=x+∇ut(x)=qt+Bt(x−mα),Bt∈S++d.T_t(x)\eqdef x+\nabla u_t(x) = q_t+B_t(x-m_\alpha), \qquad B_t\in\mathbb S_{++}^d .Tt​(x):=x+∇ut​(x)=qt​+Bt​(x−mα​),Bt​∈S++d​.
(95)

Taking the spatial gradient of the continuous ε\varepsilonε-Sinkhorn PDE removes the additive gauge. Since

F(x)=12⟨x−mα,Σα−1(x−mα)⟩+cst,G(y)=12⟨y−mβ,Σβ−1(y−mβ)⟩+cst,F(x)=\frac12\langle x-m_\alpha,\Sigma_\alpha^{-1}(x-m_\alpha)\rangle+\mathrm{cst}, \qquad G(y)=\frac12\langle y-m_\beta,\Sigma_\beta^{-1}(y-m_\beta)\rangle+\mathrm{cst},F(x)=21​⟨x−mα​,Σα−1​(x−mα​)⟩+cst,G(y)=21​⟨y−mβ​,Σβ−1​(y−mβ​)⟩+cst,
(96)

coefficient matching in the identity ∂tTt=∇∂tut\partial_tT_t=\nabla\partial_tu_t∂t​Tt​=∇∂t​ut​ gives

B˙t=Σα−1−BtΣβ−1Bt,q˙t=−BtΣβ−1(qt−mβ).\dot B_t=\Sigma_\alpha^{-1}-B_t\Sigma_\beta^{-1}B_t, \qquad \dot q_t=-B_t\Sigma_\beta^{-1}(q_t-m_\beta).B˙t​=Σα−1​−Bt​Σβ−1​Bt​,q˙​t​=−Bt​Σβ−1​(qt​−mβ​).
(97)

Thus the parabolic Monge--Ampere equation reduces, on the Gaussian ansatz, to a Riccati evolution for the linear part of the transport. The image mean is qtq_tqt​, and the image covariance is

Σt=BtΣαBt,Σ˙t=B˙tΣαBt+BtΣαB˙t.\Sigma_t=B_t\Sigma_\alpha B_t, \qquad \dot\Sigma_t=\dot B_t\Sigma_\alpha B_t+B_t\Sigma_\alpha\dot B_t.Σt​=Bt​Σα​Bt​,Σ˙t​=B˙t​Σα​Bt​+Bt​Σα​B˙t​.
(98)

At equilibrium,

BΣβ−1B=Σα−1,q=mβ,B\Sigma_\beta^{-1}B=\Sigma_\alpha^{-1}, \qquad q=m_\beta,BΣβ−1​B=Σα−1​,q=mβ​,
(99)

which is equivalent to BΣαB=ΣβB\Sigma_\alpha B=\Sigma_\betaBΣα​B=Σβ​. The stationary map is therefore the Gaussian Brenier map, and the endpoint covariance is governed by the same Bures--Wasserstein geometry as in Section Entropic Optimal Transport Between Gaussians. This Gaussian reduction should be viewed as the finite-dimensional covariance shadow of the vanishing-temperature continuous Sinkhorn limit, not as the fixed-temperature Gaussian Sinkhorn formula itself.

In one dimension the flow reduces to

∂tut(x)=log⁡(1+ut′′(x))−G(x+ut′(x))+F(x)−rˉt,\partial_tu_t(x) = \log(1+u_t''(x))-G(x+u_t'(x))+F(x)-\bar r_t,∂t​ut​(x)=log(1+ut′′​(x))−G(x+ut′​(x))+F(x)−rˉt​,
(100)

as long as 1+ut′′>01+u_t''>01+ut′′​>0. This scalar case is useful for visualization because the potential curves can be plotted directly and the positivity condition is exactly the monotonicity of x↦x+ut′(x)x\mapsto x+u_t'(x)x↦x+ut′​(x).

Monotone Clearing Beyond Variational Sinkhorn¶

The preceding convergence mechanisms mostly used variational structure: Sinkhorn is alternating KL projection, coordinate ascent on a dual objective, or a contraction in a projective metric. There is another, more algebraic, convergence mechanism which keeps the scaling form but discards the existence of an objective. In Galichon’s equilibrium-flow viewpoint, and in related work on substitutability and inverse isotonicity, one studies nonlinear market-clearing equations whose Jacobian has a substitute sign structure Galichon & Jacquet, 2024Galichon et al., 2022. This is the nonlinear analogue of the classical theory of nonsingular M-matrices and M-functions Moré & Rheinboldt, 1973Plemmons, 1977. The relevance for OT is that Sinkhorn is the canonical scaling example, but the same monotone clearing proof also covers fixed-point equations that are not first-order conditions of any convex regularized transport problem.

Two-block clearing maps¶

Write the unknowns as two blocks z=(u,v)∈Rn×Rmz=(u,v)\in\RR^n\times\RR^mz=(u,v)∈Rn×Rm, where uuu and vvv will be signed log-scalings, and let

Q(z)=(Qα(u,v),Qβ(u,v))∈Rn×Rm.Q(z)=(Q^\alpha(u,v),Q^\beta(u,v))\in\RR^n\times\RR^m.Q(z)=(Qα(u,v),Qβ(u,v))∈Rn×Rm.
(101)

The parallel coordinate-clearing map TTT is defined by solving, for each coordinate,

Qℓ(Tℓ(z),z−ℓ)=0,1≤ℓ≤n+m.Q_\ell(T_\ell(z),z_{-\ell})=0, \qquad 1\leq \ell\leq n+m.Qℓ​(Tℓ​(z),z−ℓ​)=0,1≤ℓ≤n+m.
(102)

This is the Jacobi version: all coordinates are cleared against the old values of the other coordinates. In two-block scaling problems, all coordinates in uuu decouple when vvv is fixed, and all coordinates in vvv decouple when uuu is fixed. The more common alternating Sinkhorn sweep is the Gauss--Seidel composition of these two block clearings; the order argument below is stated for the parallel map to keep the notation short. The same construction extends to any finite number of blocks.

Definition: Z-functions and M-functions

Let D⊂RND\subset\RR^ND⊂RN be an order interval. A map Q:D→RNQ:D\to\RR^NQ:D→RN is diagonally isotone if Qℓ(zℓ,z−ℓ)Q_\ell(z_\ell,z_{-\ell})Qℓ​(zℓ​,z−ℓ​) is nondecreasing in zℓz_\ellzℓ​ for every ℓ\ellℓ. It is a Z-function if increasing the other coordinates cannot increase the ℓ\ellℓ-th component:

z−ℓ≤z−ℓ′⟹Qℓ(zℓ,z−ℓ)≥Qℓ(zℓ,z−ℓ′).z_{-\ell}\leq z'_{-\ell} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_\ell(z_\ell,z_{-\ell})\geq Q_\ell(z_\ell,z'_{-\ell}).z−ℓ​≤z−ℓ′​⟹Qℓ​(zℓ​,z−ℓ​)≥Qℓ​(zℓ​,z−ℓ′​).
(103)

For a C1C^1C1 map this means ∂Qℓ/∂zk≤0\partial Q_\ell/\partial z_k\leq0∂Qℓ​/∂zk​≤0 for k≠ℓk\neq\ellk=ℓ. An M-function is a Z-function that is inverse isotone:

Q(z)≤Q(z′)⟹z≤z′.Q(z)\leq Q(z')\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z\leq z'.Q(z)≤Q(z′)⟹z≤z′.
(104)

A vector zzz is a subsolution if Q(z)≤0Q(z)\leq0Q(z)≤0, and a supersolution if Q(z)≥0Q(z)\geq0Q(z)≥0.

The M-function assumption says that cross-effects have the sign of substitutes, and that own effects dominate them strongly enough to prevent a global reversal of order. Galichon, Samuelson and Vernet formulate this idea through nonreversingness and unified gross substitutes; for single-valued maps this is the inverse-isotone structure used below. A degenerate M0M_0M0​-function keeps the same order structure but allows a null gauge direction, which is exactly what happens for balanced Sinkhorn before a potential normalization is imposed.

Theorem: Monotone convergence of coordinate clearing

Let D=[z‾,z‾]⊂RND=[\underline z,\overline z]\subset\RR^ND=[z​,z]⊂RN be a closed order interval, with z‾\underline zz​ a subsolution and z‾\overline zz a supersolution. Assume that Q:D→RNQ:D\to\RR^NQ:D→RN is continuous, diagonally isotone and an M-function. Assume also that, for every z∈Dz\in Dz∈D and every ℓ\ellℓ, the scalar clearing equation Qℓ(ξ,z−ℓ)=0Q_\ell(\xi,z_{-\ell})=0Qℓ​(ξ,z−ℓ​)=0 has a unique solution ξ∈[z‾ℓ,z‾ℓ]\xi\in[\underline z_\ell,\overline z_\ell]ξ∈[z​ℓ​,zℓ​]. Then Q(z)=0Q(z)=0Q(z)=0 has a unique solution z⋆∈Dz^\star\in Dz⋆∈D. The Jacobi coordinate-clearing iterates starting from any subsolution in DDD increase monotonically to z⋆z^\starz⋆, while those starting from any supersolution in DDD decrease monotonically to z⋆z^\starz⋆.

Proof

Let TTT be the coordinate-clearing map. If z∈Dz\in Dz∈D is a subsolution, then Qℓ(zℓ,z−ℓ)≤0=Qℓ(Tℓ(z),z−ℓ)Q_\ell(z_\ell,z_{-\ell})\leq0=Q_\ell(T_\ell(z),z_{-\ell})Qℓ​(zℓ​,z−ℓ​)≤0=Qℓ​(Tℓ​(z),z−ℓ​). Diagonal isotonicity and uniqueness of the scalar zero give zℓ≤Tℓ(z)z_\ell\leq T_\ell(z)zℓ​≤Tℓ​(z) for every ℓ\ellℓ, hence z≤T(z)z\leq T(z)z≤T(z). Since QQQ is a Z-function,

Qℓ(T(z))≤Qℓ(Tℓ(z),z−ℓ)=0,Q_\ell(T(z))\leq Q_\ell(T_\ell(z),z_{-\ell})=0,Qℓ​(T(z))≤Qℓ​(Tℓ​(z),z−ℓ​)=0,
(105)

so T(z)T(z)T(z) is again a subsolution. Since every subsolution lies below every supersolution by inverse isotonicity, T(z)≤z‾T(z)\leq\overline zT(z)≤z, and therefore T(z)∈DT(z)\in DT(z)∈D. The supersolution argument is the same with all inequalities reversed. The lower and upper iterates are thus monotone and trapped in the compact interval DDD. Their limits exist, and passing to the limit in Qℓ(zℓk+1,z−ℓk)=0Q_\ell(z_\ell^{k+1},z_{-\ell}^k)=0Qℓ​(zℓk+1​,z−ℓk​)=0 gives Q(z⋆)=0Q(z^\star)=0Q(z⋆)=0. If zzz and z′z'z′ were two zeros in DDD, inverse isotonicity applied in both directions gives z=z′z=z'z=z′.

Proposition: Smooth M-matrix certificate

Let D⊂RND\subset\RR^ND⊂RN be a convex order interval and let Q:D→RNQ:D\to\RR^NQ:D→RN be C1C^1C1. Assume that DQ(z)DQ(z)DQ(z) has nonpositive off-diagonal entries for every z∈Dz\in Dz∈D. If there exists λ≫0\lambda\gg0λ≫0 such that

λ⊤DQ(z)≫0for all z∈D,\lambda^\top DQ(z)\gg0 \qquad\text{for all }z\in D,λ⊤DQ(z)≫0for all z∈D,
(106)

or equivalently

λℓ∂Qℓ∂zℓ(z)>∑k≠ℓλk∣∂Qk∂zℓ(z)∣,1≤ℓ≤N,\lambda_\ell\frac{\partial Q_\ell}{\partial z_\ell}(z) > \sum_{k\neq \ell}\lambda_k \left|\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial z_\ell}(z)\right|, \qquad 1\leq \ell\leq N,λℓ​∂zℓ​∂Qℓ​​(z)>k=ℓ∑​λk​∣∣​∂zℓ​∂Qk​​(z)∣∣​,1≤ℓ≤N,
(107)

then QQQ is an M-function on DDD.

Proof

The off-diagonal sign gives the Z-property by integrating the partial derivatives along coordinatewise increasing segments. The displayed inequalities imply that each DQ(z)DQ(z)DQ(z) is a strictly weighted column diagonally dominant Z-matrix, hence a nonsingular M-matrix; in particular its inverse is nonnegative for each fixed zzz Plemmons, 1977. For two points z,z′∈Dz,z'\in Dz,z′∈D, set

A=∫01DQ(z′+t(z−z′)) dt.A=\int_0^1 DQ\big(z'+t(z-z')\big)\,dt .A=∫01​DQ(z′+t(z−z′))dt.
(108)

The matrix AAA has the same Z-sign pattern and the same strict weighted diagonal dominance, so it is again a nonsingular M-matrix and A−1≥0A^{-1}\geq0A−1≥0. Since Q(z)−Q(z′)=A(z−z′)Q(z)-Q(z')=A(z-z')Q(z)−Q(z′)=A(z−z′), the implication Q(z)≤Q(z′)Q(z)\leq Q(z')Q(z)≤Q(z′) gives z−z′=A−1(Q(z)−Q(z′))≤0z-z'=A^{-1}(Q(z)-Q(z'))\leq0z−z′=A−1(Q(z)−Q(z′))≤0. This is inverse isotonicity. The positive diagonal entries also give diagonal isotonicity.

Sinkhorn as the canonical M0M_0M0​-system¶

Let K=exp⁡(−C/ϵ)>0K=\exp(-C/\epsilon)>0K=exp(−C/ϵ)>0 and write

Pij=riKijsj,ri=eui,sj=e−vj.\P_{ij}=r_iK_{ij}s_j, \qquad r_i=e^{u_i},\qquad s_j=e^{-v_j}.Pij​=ri​Kij​sj​,ri​=eui​,sj​=e−vj​.
(109)

The signed convention v=−log⁡sv=-\log sv=−logs makes the clearing equations

Qiα(u,v)=∑jKijeui−vj−ai,Qjβ(u,v)=bj−∑iKijeui−vj.Q_i^\alpha(u,v)=\sum_jK_{ij}e^{u_i-v_j}-a_i, \qquad Q_j^\beta(u,v)=b_j-\sum_iK_{ij}e^{u_i-v_j}.Qiα​(u,v)=j∑​Kij​eui​−vj​−ai​,Qjβ​(u,v)=bj​−i∑​Kij​eui​−vj​.
(110)

Then Q=0Q=0Q=0 is exactly P1=a\P\mathbf 1=aP1=a and P⊤1=b\P^\top\mathbf 1=bP⊤1=b, and coordinate clearing gives the usual Sinkhorn scalings

ri+=ai∑jKijsj,sj+=bj∑iKijri.r_i^+=\frac{a_i}{\sum_jK_{ij}s_j}, \qquad s_j^+=\frac{b_j}{\sum_iK_{ij}r_i}.ri+​=∑j​Kij​sj​ai​​,sj+​=∑i​Kij​ri​bj​​.
(111)

The Jacobian has positive diagonal entries and nonpositive off-diagonal entries. Its column sums vanish, reflecting the gauge invariance (u,v)↦(u+c1,v+c1)(u,v)\mapsto(u+c\mathbf 1,v+c\mathbf 1)(u,v)↦(u+c1,v+c1). Thus balanced Sinkhorn is naturally an M0M_0M0​-system. Fixing one log-scaling coordinate turns the reduced Jacobian into a principal minor of the weighted bipartite graph Laplacian. Under connected support, automatic here because K>0K>0K>0, it is a nonsingular M-matrix. This complements the variational and Hilbert-metric proofs above, and also connects Sinkhorn scaling with choice models Qu et al., 2023.

Example: Lossy Sinkhorn clearing with outside options

The following OT-shaped clearing model is deliberately minimal. It keeps a positive transport kernel and multiplicative scalings, but introduces outside options and lossy arrivals. It should be read as a toy absorptive matching model rather than as a new transport distance. Let 0<ηij≤10<\eta_{ij}\leq10<ηij​≤1, σi>0\sigma_i>0σi​>0, τj>0\tau_j>0τj​>0, and set

Pij=riKijsj,ri=eui,sj=e−vj.\P_{ij}=r_i\K_{ij}s_j,\qquad r_i=e^{u_i},\qquad s_j=e^{-v_j}.Pij​=ri​Kij​sj​,ri​=eui​,sj​=e−vj​.
(112)

The clearing equations are

σiri+∑jPij=ai,τjsj+∑iηijPij=bj.\sigma_i r_i+\sum_jP_{ij}=a_i, \qquad \tau_j s_j+\sum_i\eta_{ij}\P_{ij}=b_j.σi​ri​+j∑​Pij​=ai​,τj​sj​+i∑​ηij​Pij​=bj​.
(113)

They say that source mass can exit through an outside sink, while target demand can be met either by effective arrivals or by a local outside source. The coordinate-clearing update is still Sinkhorn-like:

ri+=aiσi+∑jKijsj,sj+=bjτj+∑iηijKijri.r_i^+=\frac{a_i}{\sigma_i+\sum_j\K_{ij}s_j}, \qquad s_j^+=\frac{b_j}{\tau_j+\sum_i\eta_{ij}\K_{ij}r_i}.ri+​=σi​+∑j​Kij​sj​ai​​,sj+​=τj​+∑i​ηij​Kij​ri​bj​​.
(114)

In the variables (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), the off-diagonal derivatives again have the Z-sign. On the invariant domain ri≤ai/σir_i\leq a_i/\sigma_iri​≤ai​/σi​, the simple sufficient condition

τj>∑i(1−ηij)Kijaiσi,1≤j≤m,\tau_j>\sum_i(1-\eta_{ij})\K_{ij}\frac{a_i}{\sigma_i}, \qquad 1\leq j\leq m,τj​>i∑​(1−ηij​)Kij​σi​ai​​,1≤j≤m,
(115)

implies the weighted diagonal-dominance certificate 1⊤DQ≫0\ones^\top DQ\gg01⊤DQ≫0, hence Proposition Proposition: Smooth M-matrix certificate shows that the system is an M-function on that domain. Indeed, for the clearing map Qiα=σiri+∑jPij−aiQ_i^\alpha=\sigma_i r_i+\sum_jP_{ij}-a_iQiα​=σi​ri​+∑j​Pij​−ai​ and Qjβ=bj−τjsj−∑iηijPijQ_j^\beta=b_j-\tau_j s_j-\sum_i\eta_{ij}\P_{ij}Qjβ​=bj​−τj​sj​−∑i​ηij​Pij​, the column sums of the Jacobian are

σiri+∑j(1−ηij)Pij>0,τjsj−∑i(1−ηij)Pij=sj(τj−∑i(1−ηij)Kijri)>0.\sigma_i r_i+\sum_j(1-\eta_{ij})\P_{ij}>0, \qquad \tau_j s_j-\sum_i(1-\eta_{ij})\P_{ij} = s_j\left(\tau_j-\sum_i(1-\eta_{ij})\K_{ij}r_i\right)>0.σi​ri​+j∑​(1−ηij​)Pij​>0,τj​sj​−i∑​(1−ηij​)Pij​=sj​(τj​−i∑​(1−ηij​)Kij​ri​)>0.
(116)

The model is generally non-variational. If Q=∇EQ=\nabla\mathcal EQ=∇E for a C2C^2C2 potential, the cross-partials would satisfy

∂Qiα∂vj=∂Qjβ∂ui.\frac{\partial Q_i^\alpha}{\partial v_j} = \frac{\partial Q_j^\beta}{\partial u_i}.∂vj​∂Qiα​​=∂ui​∂Qjβ​​.
(117)

Here this would force −Pij=−ηijPij-\P_{ij}=-\eta_{ij}\P_{ij}−Pij​=−ηij​Pij​ on every active arc, hence ηij=1\eta_{ij}=1ηij​=1. Lossy arrivals therefore destroy exactness of the one-form ∑ℓQℓ  dzℓ\sum_\ell Q_\ell\,\d z_\ell∑ℓ​Qℓ​dzℓ​, while preserving the monotone clearing structure.
